exercises.prompt: Why is `Kiln.Free` placed in a `finally` block rather than simply at the end of the program?

options.label: So that the object is freed even if an exception leaves the try block early
options.feedback: Yes. finally runs on every way out of the try block, normal or exceptional.

options.label: Because Free may only be called inside a finally block
options.feedback: Not yet: Free can be called anywhere. finally is about guaranteeing that it is called.

options.label: To catch any exception raised by the sensor
options.feedback: Not yet: finally does not catch exceptions; it runs cleanup and lets the exception continue. Catching is what except does.

hints: What would happen to the object if SetCelsius raised an exception and nothing caught it?
exercises.solution: A `finally` block runs whether the `try` block finishes normally or because of an exception, and it does not stop the exception. Putting `Free` there guarantees the object is freed on **every** path. That is the create-try-finally-free pattern.

exercises.prompt: In the sensor program, the samples become `(45.0, 40.0, 50.5)`. How many `ALARM` lines are printed?

feedback.message: Not yet: the setter fires the alarm only when the temperature is greater than 40, and 40.0 is not.

hints: Look at the condition in SetCelsius: FCelsius > 40.
exercises.solution: 45.0 and 50.5 are above 40 and trigger the event; 40.0 is not greater than 40. So **2** alarms. (The program printed them before each corresponding reading line, because the event fires inside the setter.)

exercises.prompt: A fifth employee, `THourly.Create('Eero', 18.00, 0)`, is added to the team. What does the line `Hourly staff:` show?
hints: `E is THourly` is true for every hourly employee, whatever their hours.
exercises.solution: Bilal, Dagny and Eero are `THourly` objects, so the count is **3**. Eero's pay is 0.00 and the total is unchanged.

feedback.message: Not yet: something else happens when F is given a new object.

hints: What happens to the INR formatter's reference count when F is assigned the plain formatter?
exercises.solution: Assigning the plain formatter to `F` drops the INR formatter's reference count to zero, so it is destroyed at once and its destructor prints **(INR formatter freed)** before `done`. (The first line was `INR 99,999.99`.)

feedback.message: Close: the %n format adds thousands separators.

hints: `%.2n` prints two decimals with thousands separators.
exercises.solution: 9 999 999 cents is 99 999.99, and `%.2n` formats it with a thousands separator and two decimals: **INR 99,999.99** (with the default format settings).

exercises.prompt: A class `TAccount` declares a field `FBalance` in a plain `private` section. Which code can read `FBalance` directly?

options.label: TAccount's methods and any other code in the same unit
options.feedback: Yes. Object Pascal's private is unit-wide; strict private is class-only.

options.label: Only TAccount's own methods
options.feedback: Not yet: that is strict private. Plain private is visible to the whole unit.

options.label: TAccount's methods and its descendants' methods in any unit
options.feedback: Not yet: that describes protected (more or less). Private is not visible to descendants in other units.

hints: Object Pascal has both private and strict private.
exercises.solution: Plain `private` members are visible to the class **and to all code in the same unit**, a historical convenience. Use `strict private` when you want only the class's own methods to have access.

exercises.prompt: `TA` declares `function Name: string; virtual;` returning 'A'. `TB = class(TA)` declares `function Name: string;` (without `override`) returning 'B'. What does `X := TB.Create; WriteLn(X.Name);` print when `X` is declared as `TA`?

options.label: A
options.feedback: Yes. Without override, TB.Name hides TA.Name instead of replacing it in the virtual method table.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Not yet: that would need override. The compiler even warns that an inherited method is hidden.

options.label: It does not compile
options.feedback: Not yet: it compiles with a warning, which is what makes the mistake dangerous.

hints: What did Free Pascal's warning say?
exercises.solution: Without `override`, `TB.Name` is a new method that merely hides `TA.Name`. A call through a `TA` reference uses the virtual method table entry, which still points to `TA.Name`, so it prints **A**. Free Pascal warns `An inherited method is hidden`; treat that warning as an error.
